newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: S.Leone soldiers held for piracy, strike ends.
newsitem.headline: S.Leone soldiers held for piracy, strike ends.

text.p: Fishermen working off Sierra Leone on Tuesday cancelled a strike protesting a surge in piracy after a navy patrol arrested five soldiers caught raiding a fishing vessel, fisheries officials said.

The capture of the soldiers on Monday on Banana Island near Freetown prompted the 1,500 fishing workers to call off their 10-day-old strike intended to put pressure on the government to act against mounting piracy on fishing vessels off Sierra Leone.
The navy said on Tuesday the soldiers were in detention. "They attacked a fishing trawler on Banana Island," an officer said.
Fishing officials said the unnamed vessel belonged to Okekey Fishing Co Ltd, one of Sierra Leone's biggest fishing firms.

Striking trawler workers from Sierra Leone, Senegal, Guinea Bissau, Spain, Portugal and South Korea, said on Tuesday they were returning to sea in recognition of efforts by the government to deal with piracy.
"We are calling off the strike because after one week of negotiation they have doubled naval units patrolling the territorial waters," union spokesman Jonas Coleman said.
"The fact that the patrol units yesterday captured five government soldiers attacking a trawler captained by a South Korean off Freetown coast helped a great deal," he said.
Jonas said police had also stepped up prosecution of piracy cases before the courts in Sierra Leone.

Coleman, deputy managing director of Okekey Fishing Co, said another South Korean captain on one of two trawlers attacked in broad daylight last week was recovering in a Freetown hospital from serious injuries.
"He had been beaten senseless and then thrown from the boat's top deck into the main hold," he said.

He said the alarming increase in piracy off the Sierra Leone was damaging the country's fishing industry, one of the few sectors still operating. Much of the mining-based economy has been devastated by a five-year-old civil war.
"Pirates scare away foreign vessels from Sierra Leone. They also raid our own boats and steal thousands of dollars worth of fish and equipment almost daily," he added.

A boat owners' association in Spain and the Canary Islands called on the Sierra Leone government last month to act against piracy. It said in a letter to the Ministry of Maritime Resources that the pirates were heavily armed, systematically organised and carried out their attacks at regular intervals.

In July the sub-regional fishing committee comprising Senegal, Gambia, Mauritania, Guinea, Guinea Bissau and Sierra Leone agreed to the Freetown government's request to use committee planes to survey the coast.
The first flights operated in the last week of August and early September but it was not clear if these had been followed up with further flights.
